timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: How do hackers even find targets?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Reconnaissance, Peter. It's the first phase of any attack. Attackers gather information about their target before launching a single exploit. And most of it is completely legal.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: OSINT - Open Source Intelligence. Job postings reveal your tech stack. LinkedIn reveals employee names and roles. GitHub might have exposed API keys. Shodan shows your internet-facing devices.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: And much more. Google dorking can find exposed login pages, misconfigured databases, and sensitive documents. 'site:example.com filetype:pdf password' can be devastatingly effective.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: The 2020 Twitter hack started with reconnaissance. Attackers found employee contact info on LinkedIn, then used phone-based social engineering to get VPN credentials.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: So I should clean up my online presence?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Absolutely. Audit what your organization exposes. Remove old job postings, lock down GitHub repos, monitor for leaked credentials, and train employees on social engineering.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Active recon involves scanning - Nmap for port scanning, directory brute-forcing, vulnerability scanning. This is where you cross from passive to potentially illegal territory.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Describe the phases of reconnaissance for a web application target. Include both passive and active techniques. This question comes up in every pentest interview.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Remember: the attacker who knows the most about you wins. Limit your attack surface by controlling what's exposed.
